pitfall_counterexample:
Witness: k = 1 (and k = 2). The verbatim sentence pins two integers simultaneously: the new system phi' "contain[s] exactly two equations", so size(phi') = 2, and the justification asserted is size(phi') < k, i.e. 2 < k. The inductive step is applied to a system phi of size n = k+1, so it must cover every k >= 1.

- k = 1: phi has 2 equations. The asserted inequality reads 2 < 1 -> FALSE. Moreover even the weakest decrease that could make the recursion well founded, size(phi') < size(phi) = k+1, reads 2 < 2 -> FALSE. At k = 1 the "apply the induction hypothesis to the first k equations" step is the identity (one equation collapses to itself), so phi' is literally the same 2-equation system one started with: the step maps the two-equation case to itself.
- k = 2: phi has 3 equations, phi' has 2. The asserted inequality reads 2 < 2 -> FALSE.

Exhaustive scan over k = 1..100000 finds failures at exactly k in {1, 2} for the literal assertion and exactly k = 1 for the charitable "strictly smaller than phi" reading; the assertion is true for all k >= 3, i.e. the decrease holds only away from the small cases.

Independent confirmation via the induced call graph (CHECK C): a call on a system of size n spawns call(n-1) (first k equations) and call(2) (the new phi'). Exhaustively closing this relation for every start size n = 2..500 and every candidate base-case threshold b = 0..5 yields explicit cycles for b = 0 (call(1) -> call(2) -> call(1) -> ...) and b = 1 (call(2) -> call(2) -> ...). The recursion therefore never reaches a base case: it re-enters the two-equation system forever. The only thresholds b >= 2 that terminate are exactly those that assume the two-equation case outright, i.e. assume the genuinely hard case the induction was meant to establish.
